content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a guideline on school health services, which includes a systematic review of the effectiveness and acceptability of comprehensive school health services (SHS). This review, detailed in Web Annex D, outlines the methodology used to assess the impact of SHS on health outcomes, service coverage, and stakeholder satisfaction. The review was conducted in compliance with PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) standards and evaluated both quantitative and qualitative data, as well as the economic costs and benefits of SHS. The systematic review posed two key research questions: (1) Are comprehensive SHS effective in improving health outcomes or increasing health service coverage for school-aged children and adolescents? (2) Are comprehensive SHS acceptable to stakeholders, including children, adolescents, parents, teachers, and policymakers? To address these questions, six databases were searched, and a pilot search strategy was used to identify studies related to the concept of school health services. The search strategy was designed to capture studies on the effectiveness, acceptability, and economic aspects of SHS. The review included studies that met specific criteria, such as interventions involving at least one clinical strategy (e.g., screening, preventive interventions like immunization, or clinical assessments leading to care or referral). These interventions could also include health promotion, health education, or support for other pillars of health-promoting schools. The services had to be delivered or supervised by a health worker dedicated to school-going learners. Interventions delivered solely by trained teachers were excluded. The outcomes considered for the effectiveness review included coverage (e.g., the proportion of the target population participating in the intervention), policy uptake, responsiveness to unmet needs (including equity issues), and health and development outcomes. These outcomes encompassed areas such as positive development (e.g., health-seeking behavior, self-esteem), prevention of unintentional injuries, violence, sexual and reproductive health, communicable and non-communicable diseases, nutrition, mental health, and substance use. Educational outcomes, such as school attendance and health literacy, were also evaluated. Critical outcomes were defined as those related to short-term mortality or morbidity requiring major health service expenditure or improvements in key educational metrics. Important outcomes included those affecting chronic morbidity, the academic climate, or SHS coverage. For the acceptability review, outcomes included access and use of SHS, user satisfaction, preferences for school-based versus other settings, quality of services (e.g., barriers to access, confidentiality, respect, and stigma), relevance to students' health issues, fidelity to program guidelines, cultural sensitivity, and feasibility of implementation. Provider perspectives, such as challenges in service availability and willingness to pay, were also considered. The review process involved screening 8,523 records, of which 443 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. High-quality evidence was prioritized, including systematic reviews, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), and non-randomized controlled studies (NCSs). Observational studies were included as supplementary data when high-quality evidence was insufficient. Ultimately, 18 NCSs and 19 observational studies were included, with additional economic studies identified for cost-effectiveness analysis. No eligible RCTs were found. The quality of included studies was rigorously appraised using established tools, such as AMSTAR 2 for systematic reviews, the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies, and the Critical Skills Appraisal Programme checklist for economic evaluations. Qualitative studies were assessed based on credibility, transferability, dependability, and confirmability. Data extraction was conducted using a pre-specified and pilot-tested spreadsheet, capturing details such as study design, population characteristics, interventions, comparators, outcomes, and analysis methods. Results were synthesized narratively and thematically, with quantitative data pooled where appropriate. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic, and findings were presented in tables for consistency. The review findings contribute to the WHO guideline on school health services, providing evidence on the effectiveness, acceptability, and economic implications of SHS. This guideline aims to support policymakers and stakeholders in implementing evidence-based interventions to improve the health and well-being of school-aged children and adolescents globally.
